chapters.title: Chapter 2: Global Cycles That Shaped Modern Markets

lessons.title: Stagflation to the Great Disinflation: The 1970s to 2000

body.text: Inflation is a bear market that never shows up on the index chart. From 1966 to 1982 the Dow lost about a fifth of its value in dollars and about three quarters in real terms. Then falling inflation powered one of the greatest bull markets in history. Largely the same companies, opposite tide.

children.text: Lesson 2.2 ended in 1966, with the Dow just short of 1,000. This lesson covers the 34 years that followed, and they split cleanly into two halves. The first half, to 1982, was a secular bear market driven by inflation. The second half, to 2000, was a secular bull market driven by disinflation, meaning inflation falling steadily. Between them they show the most important macro force behind long market cycles: the level and direction of inflation and interest rates.

markDefs.definition: A painful combination of high inflation, weak economic growth and high unemployment. The term is usually credited to the British politician Iain Macleod in 1965.

children.text: In the late 1960s the US government spent heavily on both the Vietnam War and domestic programmes without raising taxes enough to pay for them, and inflation began to creep up. Then a series of shocks turned a slow rise into a fever. Economists at the time believed high inflation and high unemployment could not persist together. The 1970s proved them wrong, and gave the world a new word:

body.title: The inflation decade and its cure

events.title: The Nixon shock
events.description: President Nixon suspends the conversion of US dollars into gold. The Bretton Woods system from Lesson 2.2 breaks down, and by 1973 major currencies float freely. The anchor that had limited money creation is gone.

events.title: First oil shock
events.description: Arab oil producers impose an embargo on the US and other countries after the Yom Kippur War. The price of oil roughly quadruples within months, feeding straight into transport, fertiliser and manufacturing costs worldwide.

events.title: A brutal bear market
events.description: The Dow falls about 45%, from roughly 1,052 to 578. Inflation reaches double digits in 1974 while the economy shrinks.

events.title: Second oil shock
events.description: The Iranian Revolution disrupts supply and oil prices more than double again. US inflation, which never properly came down after 1974, surges.

events.title: Volcker arrives
events.description: Paul Volcker becomes chairman of the Federal Reserve and shifts policy to target the money supply, allowing interest rates to rise as high as needed to break inflation.

events.title: The peak of the fever
events.description: US consumer price inflation hits 14.8% in March 1980. Gold reaches about $850 an ounce in January 1980. Short-term interest rates approach 20%, and the 10-year US government bond yield peaks near 15.8% in September 1981.

events.title: The cure hurts, then works
events.description: The US suffers a deep recession, with unemployment reaching 10.8% at the end of the year. Inflation falls sharply. In August 1982 the Dow bottoms near 777, below where it had been 16 years earlier, and a new bull market begins.

stats.label: Gold
stats.context: Official price before 1971 to the January 1980 peak

stats.label: Dow, Feb 1966 to Aug 1982
stats.context: Down about 22% in dollars, about 74% after inflation

children.text: A fall from 995 to 777 over 16 years sounds disappointing but survivable. It was far worse than that. US consumer prices roughly tripled over the same period, so each dollar in 1982 bought about a third of what it had in 1966. Dividends softened the blow but did not come close to closing the gap. Inflation hurts shares in three ways at once: it raises the interest rates that bonds and deposits pay, which makes shares less attractive by comparison; it squeezes company profit margins when costs rise faster than prices can be passed on; and it makes investors demand a lower P/E for a given stream of earnings. By 1982 the US market traded at a P/E of under 10.

body.title: Measure the Silent Bear
body.prompt: An investor's holding fell 22% in nominal terms over 16 years, meaning ₹100 became ₹78. Over the same period, consumer prices tripled, so something that cost ₹100 at the start now costs ₹300. By what percentage did the purchasing power of the holding fall? Enter the fall as a positive number, rounded to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: Real value = ₹78 ÷ 3 = ₹26 in starting-year purchasing power. Real return = 26 ÷ 100 − 1 = −74%. A 22% nominal fall became a 74% loss in what the money could actually buy. This is roughly what happened to the Dow between 1966 and 1982, before dividends.

body.text: Indian savers know the silent bear market well, just in fixed income rather than shares. In 2020-21, many one-year bank fixed deposits paid around 5%, while CPI inflation ran above 6%. A depositor who saw their balance grow was actually losing purchasing power, and after paying income tax on the interest, the real loss was bigger. The number on your statement is not the number that matters.

children.text: The Nifty Fifty: Great Companies at Any Price

Inside this secular bear market sat one of history's most instructive mini-bubbles. In the early 1970s, American fund managers crowded into a group of about 50 large, fast-growing, famous companies, including Coca-Cola, IBM, Xerox, McDonald's, Avon and Polaroid. They were nicknamed the Nifty Fifty, which has no connection to NSE's Nifty 50 index. They were called one-decision stocks: buy them and never sell, because great businesses would always grow into their valuations. Many of them were genuinely excellent businesses. The problem, once again, was price.

body.title: The Nifty Fifty story vs what actually happened

columns.label: The story in 1972
points: These companies are so dominant that any price is justified
Earnings growth will make today's high P/E look cheap within a few years
You never need to sell a great business
Everyone serious owns them, so they must be safe

columns.label: What happened in 1973 to 1974
points: Inflation and rising rates crushed the multiples investors would pay
Many of the group fell far more than the overall market
Some, like Polaroid and Xerox, later lost their competitive edge entirely
Even the survivors took many years to justify their 1972 prices

body.label: The price of certainty
body.value: Polaroid: P/E of roughly 90 in 1972, share price down about 90% by 1974
body.context: One of the most admired technology companies of its day. Its business kept operating, but the multiple collapsed, and the company eventually went bankrupt in 2001.

body.title: The Indian Quality Trap
body.question: A well-loved Indian consumer company trades at a P/E of 80. Over the next five years its earnings grow a very healthy 15% a year, roughly doubling. By the end, investors are only willing to pay a P/E of 40. Roughly what total return did a shareholder earn on price over those five years?
options: About −50%, matching the fall in P/E
body.explanation: Earnings grow 1.15 to the power 5, about 2.01 times. The P/E halves, a factor of 0.5. Price changes by 2.01 × 0.5, about 1.006 times, so the shareholder earns roughly nothing on price for five years, despite excellent business performance. This is the Nifty Fifty lesson. Check the P/E history of India's most popular consumer stocks on screener.in and you will see multiples in this range have occurred.

children.text: Volcker's high rates caused a painful recession, but they broke inflation's grip and, crucially, broke the expectation that inflation would keep rising. Once that happened, everything that had worked against shares in the 1970s went into reverse for almost two decades. Inflation drifted lower, bond yields fell from their 1981 peak, and investors were willing to pay steadily higher multiples for earnings. Add falling oil prices from the mid 1980s, lower tax rates, globalisation, the end of the Cold War, the personal computer and the internet, and you have the fuel for the longest bull market of the century.

body.title: US consumer price inflation, annual average, 1965 to 2000

children.text: Where did a fifteen-fold rise come from? Use the trend plus cycle split from Lesson 1.1. Price growth is earnings growth multiplied by the change in the P/E ratio.

US corporate earnings grew handsomely, but the P/E on the broad market also went from under 10 in 1982 to around 30 by early 2000. Roughly half of the entire bull market, in multiplicative terms, came from investors paying more for each dollar of profit. That part was a one-off gift from falling inflation and rates. It could not repeat unless inflation and rates kept falling forever, and at those prices it did not: the S&P 500 delivered a slightly negative total return over the decade that began in 2000.

body.caption: Cycles inside the disinflation bull market (Dow Jones, approximate)

cells: Includes Black Monday, 19 October 1987, when the Dow fell about 23% in a single day
Oil price spike after Iraq invades Kuwait, and a US recession
Russia defaults and the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management nearly collapses

body.text: Almost every investor who started between 1982 and 2000 learned one lesson: buy the dip, it always comes back quickly. That lesson was true for that cycle, because falling inflation and rates kept lifting multiples. Investors who carried it into 2000 at a P/E near 30 got a very different decade. The rules that worked best in one secular cycle are often exactly the rules that fail in the next.

body.caption: How the same global shocks landed in a closed Indian economy

cells: The first oil shock and poor harvests push wholesale price inflation above 25% in 1974, one of the worst inflation episodes in independent India

The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act requires most foreign-controlled companies to cut foreign shareholding to 40%. Many issue shares to Indian investors at government-controlled prices, and a generation of retail shareholders is born. Some firms, including Coca-Cola and IBM, leave India in 1977 instead
The second oil shock blows out India's import bill. In 1981 India takes a large loan from the IMF

The Sensex, launched in 1986 with a base of 100 in 1978-79, reaches 1,000 in July 1990. The slow opening of the economy in the 1980s begins, setting up the crisis and reforms of 1991 covered in Chapter 3

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The combination of high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment that defined the 1970s is called ___.
body.explanation: Stagflation is especially damaging for markets because the usual policy response to weak growth, cutting rates, makes inflation worse, while the response to inflation, raising rates, makes growth weaker.

body.title: "Equities Always Beat Inflation"
body.scenario: At a family dinner in Chennai, your uncle, a retired bank officer, says: "Shares always beat inflation over 15 years. Anyone who says otherwise doesn't understand markets." Your cousin, who has just started a ₹10,000 monthly SIP in a Nifty 50 index fund, looks reassured.
body.prompt: Is your uncle right? Use this lesson to give a fair, balanced answer, and suggest what actually matters for your cousin.
body.modelAnswer: Your uncle is right more often than not, but "always" is wrong. From 1966 to 1982 the Dow fell about 22% in dollar terms while US prices tripled, a real loss of about 74% before dividends, and even with dividends US shares lost purchasing power over that 16-year stretch. Two things made that period so bad: shares started at high valuations, and inflation rose sharply and stayed high. The reverse, low starting valuations and falling inflation from 1982, produced spectacular real returns. So the honest answer is that equities have beaten inflation over most long periods, in the US and in India, but the result depends heavily on the starting valuation and on the inflation cycle, and there have been long stretches when they did not. For your cousin, the SIP itself helps: investing a fixed amount every month for many years means buying at many different valuations rather than betting everything on one starting point. What matters is a long horizon, keeping costs low, not stopping the SIP in a bad patch, and not assuming any single decade will look like the last one.

cards.definition: High inflation combined with weak growth and high unemployment. The defining condition of the 1970s.
The August 1971 decision to end conversion of US dollars into gold, which led to the collapse of the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system.
About 50 popular US growth stocks of the early 1970s bought at very high P/Es as one-decision stocks. Many fell far more than the market in 1973 to 1974. Unrelated to NSE's Nifty 50.
The Federal Reserve's policy from 1979 of allowing interest rates to rise to around 20% to break inflation, at the cost of a deep recession.
A fall in the rate of inflation, with prices still rising but more slowly. Different from deflation, where prices actually fall.
A rise in the P/E ratio investors pay. Responsible for roughly half the US market's rise from 1982 to 2000.

body.label: MOSPI: Consumer Price Index Data
body.description: The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation publishes India's official monthly CPI inflation figures. Compare the latest number with your fixed deposit rate, after tax, to see whether your savings are growing in real terms.

children.text: While the US was enjoying the disinflation boom, another economy was living through a very different cycle. In 1989 Japan's stock market peaked at levels it would not see again for 34 years. Lesson 2.4 asks the question every long-term investor should face: what happens when a cycle refuses to turn?

body.text: Market levels, inflation rates and valuation multiples in this lesson are approximate, rounded and drawn from sources that can differ slightly. Company examples are historical illustrations only, and nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security or investment advice.

points: From 1966 to 1982 the Dow fell from about 995 to about 777, while US prices roughly tripled, a real loss of about 74% before dividends
The breakdown of Bretton Woods in 1971, two oil shocks and loose policy produced stagflation, with US inflation peaking at 14.8% in 1980
The Nifty Fifty showed that excellent companies bought at extreme P/Es can deliver terrible returns when multiples collapse
Volcker's high interest rates caused a deep recession but broke inflation, starting a disinflation bull market in which the Dow rose about 15 times from 1982 to 2000
Roughly half of that rise came from multiple expansion, a one-off gift from falling inflation and rates that could not repeat
In India, the 1970s brought inflation above 25%, and FERA share dilutions that created a new generation of retail investors
Rules that work in one secular cycle, such as always buying the dip, often fail in the next
